title: Romi's Wobbly Chairs
markdown:
Romi the badger liked everything to be just right. He was host of the Whispering Woods Talent Evening, the event the woodland waited for all year, and he meant this one to be the most proper, the most perfectly organised, the most wonderfully proper evening the trees had ever seen.

Every day he polished his spectacles, which had a habit of sliding down his long nose when he thought too hard. He smoothed his smart grey fur. He practised his most welcoming words — “Welcome, one and all!” — until they sat neatly in his mouth. He studied his list of performers until the ink looked as calm as a pond. As the moon climbed, he would nod, sure that everything was in its right place.

He pictured quiet applause, perfectly timed acts, and smooth changes from one performer to the next. He even practised bowing with just the right amount of grace, making sure his spectacles did not wobble too much.

Until one day, as the sun dappled through the trees and the air hummed, the performers began to arrive.

First into the clearing came Bartholomew Bear, chest puffed out, ready to share his longest poem. Romi greeted him with a warm smile.

“Welcome, Bartholomew. We’re so glad you’re here. Please, have a seat.”

Romi pointed to a perfectly placed chair. Bartholomew rumbled his thanks and sat. Then his brow furrowed.

“Ah, Romi,” he said, his voice deep like thunder, “I’ll be needing one extra chair for my prop. It’s a very important balloon, you see. It needs to float just so.”

Romi, always helpful, fetched another sturdy chair from the neat pile.

Because of that, the next arrivals found the clearing already a little less exact. With a swirl of bright colours, the Flutterwing butterflies came in. They were famous for their flying dance, a show of light and air, and they needed a very special arrangement of chairs for their special audience — a group of tiny, sparkling beetles who always brought their opera glasses.

Romi, his brow now a little more furrowed, checked his list and added two more chairs, placing them carefully for the beetles. The beetles settled at once, glasses gleaming, as if the extra seats had been waiting for them all along.

Because of that, Jude the duck arrived with a cheerful bouncing walk and a song already wobbling in his throat. His songs were often a little quacky, like a leaf dancing on the breeze.

“Hooray for Romi!” Jude quacked, bright eyes shining. “I’m absolutely ready to sing my latest tune! And look!” He nudged a small wooden maraca with his beak. “I’ve brought my lucky maraca. It needs its own seat, you see, so it doesn’t feel lonely while I’m performing.”

Romi, who had started the day with exactly the right number of chairs on his carefully planned list, gently nudged yet another extra chair towards Jude. His list was beginning to feel a little wiggly.

He looked at the page again, whiskers twitching. “Next,” he said quietly to himself, “is the very elegant Mrs Clover, with her delicate petal-weaving demonstration.”

Mrs Clover arrived with a woven basket overflowing with the most vibrant, sweet-smelling petals — red poppies, sunshine-yellow dandelions, and sky-blue cornflowers. She loved making quiet art, her movements as graceful and silent as a falling autumn leaf.

“Oh, Romi,” she whispered, her voice as soft as honeysuckle, “this is such a truly beautiful evening. I do hope you have enough space. My prize-winning scarlet poppy petal likes to have its own little spot for inspiration. It finds the gentle breeze quite interesting, you understand.”

Romi looked at the growing collection of chairs, scattered now. Some held poetry books. Others were wobbly with balloons. It was, he had to admit, a lot of extra chairs for a talent evening that was supposed to be the most orderly event in the woods.

Because of that, the stage began to feel less like a stage and more like a warm, friendly gathering. The neatly arranged chairs seemed to be whispering funny secrets to one another. Bartholomew’s balloon bobbed merrily, as if in time to an unheard song. Jude’s lucky maraca jiggled with happy excitement. The Flutterwing butterflies giggled among themselves, wings shimmering.

Romi took a deep, calming breath, like a sigh carried on the wind. The ancient oak trees rustled with a knowing, gentle amusement, their branches swaying as if they had seen this sort of evening before.

“Patience now,” he told himself, spectacles sliding a little further down his nose. “All will be revealed in time.”

He watched the performers chatting and laughing. The extra chairs, somehow, made the space feel warmer, more welcoming, more alive. A happy feeling bubbled up inside him. He cleared his throat, a small, proper sound that quickly turned cheerful.

“My dear friends,” he announced, his voice gaining a new warmth, “it seems we have a few more seats than I had originally planned for. And that,” he added with a broad smile, “means more friends to enjoy this wonderful show.”

Until finally, Romi the badger found himself perched on a very small, slightly wobbly stool right at the very edge of the stage. His neatly organised notes, once crisp and perfect, were now a little crumpled, tucked under his paw. The air filled with Jude’s enthusiastically wobbly singing. The sweet, delicate scent of Mrs Clover’s petals drifted around like a gentle perfume. Bartholomew’s balloon seemed to dance in time with the music. A tremor of pure joy rippled through Romi’s whiskers. This was not the proper, perfectly planned evening he had imagined. It was an evening overflowing with laughter, unexpected delights, and more than enough chairs for everyone, and then some.

Ever since then, the Whispering Woods Talent Evening has been known not only for its performances, but for Romi’s generous spirit, and for the cozy abundance of chairs always ready for one more friend.
characters: Romi (a badger), Jude (a duck), Clover (a weaver)
author: StoryGen Community
